https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Minutes of the Troy Board of Education workshop held Tuesday, May 2, 2023, in the Administration Building at 4400 Livernois, Troy, Michigan. These minutes appear in the June 13, 2023 regular meeting packet, presented for board approval. President Schmidt called the workshop to order at 6:05 p.m. In addition to Mr. Schmidt, board members Alic, Anne, Hauff, Haupt, and Wilson were present; Dr. Philippart was absent. Also in attendance were Superintendent Machesky and administrators Birmingham, DiPilato, Griffor, Harris, Pagel, Haezebrouck, and West, along with three math coordinators. The audience numbered approximately 70 community members, and a news crew and reporter were present, reflecting heightened public interest.

The dominant issue was the district's removal of honors courses. During Public Communication, sixteen residents addressed the board. The following spoke specifically about the removal of honors courses: Suril Patel; Carol Kohut; Yawen Li; Yue Xuan; Jing Dai; Steven Sheng; Curry Wu; Ruihua Han; Fabrice Smieliauskas; Kristin LaPado; Chris Kus; Jeff Schaeper; and Alex Karpowitsch. Mr. Ollie Apahidean and Ye (Denise) Ye addressed transparency in the district, and Mrs. Tracy Owens addressed an email the district had sent out to the community. Most speakers are identified in the minutes as Troy residents and district parents.

Following public comment, the board received a Business Services Update from the administration covering several forthcoming action items: a Food Service Contract Renewal; an SEC Contract; a Network Core Replacement; a Copier Replacement; a 2023 iPad Purchase; and Elementary Security Cameras. Under Teaching & Learning, the administration presented a Middle School Math Update, the curriculum topic connected to the honors-course concerns raised by the public and the reason three math coordinators attended.

No formal votes or resolutions are recorded in these workshop minutes, consistent with the study-session nature of a board workshop. The meeting was adjourned at 9:55 p.m. The minutes were respectfully submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary of the Troy Board of Education (noted as GH/jh). The workshop stands as a documented flashpoint in the community's response to curriculum changes, particularly the elimination of honors courses and related middle school math restructuring, during the 2022-23 school year.

The Troy School District Cash Position Report for the month ended May 31, 2023 reconciles the district's cash by fund group across the month. It presents four fund columns plus a total: General (funds 101, 120, 122); Special Revenue (520, 529, 530, 531); Debt Service (314, 315, 316, 320, 321); and Capital Projects (419, 423, 498, 499).

The largest components were State Aid of $12,500,483 (General $12,186,387; Special Revenue $314,097) and federal grant revenue of $4,447,861 (General $4,159,308; Special Revenue $288,553). https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
The Troy School District Statement of Revenues and Expenditures presents interim (year-to-date) financial results for the period July 1, 2022 through May 31, 2023, roughly eleven months into the fiscal year, comparing the approved budget (as of the June 13, 2023 amendment) to actual figures for the General Fund, the Consolidated Debt Service Funds, and several special revenue funds.

General Fund revenues year-to-date totaled $147,096,448 against an approved budget of $189,304,235. By source, actuals were Local $39,641,866 (budget $40,857,721), State $94,974,666 (budget $127,647,472), Federal $4,651,400 (budget $9,449,097), and Interdistrict $7,828,516 (budget $11,349,945). The State and Federal actuals sit well below budget because much of that revenue is received later in the fiscal year. General Fund expenditures totaled $159,457,690 against a $189,751,106 budget. Instruction expenditures were $102,932,163 (of a $124,803,392 budget), comprising Basic Programs $76,771,819, Added Needs $25,382,500, and Adult Education $777,843. Support Services totaled $55,863,802 (budget $64,225,331), including Pupil support $11,620,204, Instructional Staff $9,962,833, School Administration $9,461,032, Operations/Maintenance $12,486,554, Pupil Transportation $3,361,376, Central Services $3,574,554, and Athletics $2,285,233. Community Services expenditures were $183,326 and Debt Service $478,400. The General Fund thus showed revenues under expenditures of $12,361,242 year-to-date, versus a budgeted full-year shortfall of $446,871.

The Consolidated Debt Service Funds reported year-to-date revenues of $18,930,640 (budget $19,175,000), consisting of Local Sources $18,658,200 and State Sources $272,440. Expenditures were $18,317,752, of which Principal was $15,325,000, Interest $2,990,860, and Other Transactions $1,893; this left revenues over expenditures of $612,888 (against a budgeted $855,640).

The statement additionally reports the district's special revenue funds. The Food Service Fund (520) was break-even, with revenues and expenditures each at $2,068,660, funded almost entirely by federal sources ($2,068,660 federal; $0 state received of a $100,000 budget) and spending on salaries ($895,488), benefits ($539,124), and purchased services ($588,139). https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A closed-session authorizing resolution prepared for the Troy Board of Education's regular meeting on August 15, 2023, filed as agenda item 12.A. The item's stated consideration is the 'Purchase of Real Property.' Under the format, the Board must first pass a resolution to enter closed session; following passage, the Board convenes in closed session, and the document specifies that no additional business will take place afterward other than to officially adjourn the meeting.

The recommended action is to adopt the resolution, which reads: 'BE IT THEREFORE RESOLVED that, as permitted in the Michigan Open Meetings Act, Public Act 267, in accordance MCL 15.268 Section 8.1 (d) and (k) to discuss the purchase of real property.' Section 8(1)(d) of the Open Meetings Act permits a closed session to consider the purchase or lease of real property up to the point at which an option to purchase is obtained, and the cited subsection (k) covers related exempt matters. The resolution provides blank 'Moved by' and 'Supported by' lines and calls for a roll-call vote.

The roll-call list names board members Hauff, Haupt, Philippart, Schmidt, Wilson, Alic, and Anne[…] (the final entry is truncated in the record). Because this is a pre-meeting template, it records no mover, supporter, or vote tally, and it discloses no property address, purchase price, seller, or other terms — those matters would be discussed in the closed session itself. The document is purely procedural.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A staff memorandum supporting agenda item 8.A. at the Troy School District Board of Education's August 15, 2023 regular meeting, authored by Corrie Spurlin — Troy School District K-12 Vocal Music Coordinator, Elementary Vocal Music Department Chair, and Elementary Vocal Music Teacher at Schroeder Elementary — and addressed to Rick West, Assistant Superintendent, Business Services. It is dated Friday, August 4, 2023, and its subject is the 'Elementary Piano Replacement Initiative.'

The memo opens by noting that Troy's K-12 music programs are recurring recipients of the NAMM Foundation's 'Best Community for Music Education' designation. It then explains the need: the 38 institutional acoustic pianos used by the Elementary Vocal and Instrumental Music teams are in dire need of replacement, with 87% identified as beyond reasonable repair. Every piano is described as beyond its expected lifespan, only a small few meet minimum quality expectations for institutional use, and one piano poses a significant danger to staff and students and must be replaced immediately. Spurlin argues the instruments are essential instructional tools — providing consistent intonation for training students' ears, tuning, accompaniment, and vocal and instrumental instruction and performance — and that pianos beyond their useful life cannot deliver the consistent frequencies students need to build these foundational skills.

The request, made on behalf of both the Elementary Vocal and Instrumental Music teams, is for Board approval to replace all elementary-level pianos with Kawai Institutional Digital Keyboards, model CA-901, alternating instruments to the secondary level every five years or as needed. The memo frames the keyboards as a technology purchase with an 8–10 year lifespan, carrying a five-year warranty, never going out of tune, and requiring little maintenance. The CA-901 units can interface via line-out with technology upgrades underway in the district's elementary cafeterias and can be augmented through district-issued Apple devices via Bluetooth and app.

On procurement, the memo states a competitive invitation for bid was sent to three piano dealers in April, and that Kawai Piano Gallery of Bloomfield, MI provided the best quote matching expected specifications. Using Kawai Gallery's bid, the cost to replace all 38 acoustic pianos with Kawai CA-901 institutional-grade digital keyboards — including new benches, dollies, canvas covers, a five-year parts-and-labor warranty, local technician support, delivery, setup, installation, and professional hands-on learning scheduled for August 23, 2023 — totals $251,788.00. The memorandum is signed 'Respectfully submitted, Mrs. Corrie Spurlin,' with contact details CSpurlin@Troy.k12.mi.us and 248-494-0320. It serves as the justification narrative paired with the item 8.A. quotation packet and contains no resolution text or recorded vote; it is a recommendation supporting the Board's purchasing decision.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A presentation to the Troy Board of Education summarizing the data-gathering phase of the district's "Portrait of a Troy Graduate" initiative, an effort to define the traits students should display if Troy is delivering a "world class education." Input came from 308 parent surveys, an all-principals K-12 discussion, and 30-minute conversations with more than 320 students across 16 classrooms spanning four high schools, three middle schools, four elementary schools, and one preschool. The exercise found near-perfect consensus among the three groups and produced 12 graduate traits, including Visionary, Connected, and Kind, Compassionate, and Inclusive.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
A summary presentation of the data-gathering phase of Troy School District's "Portrait of a Troy Graduate" exercise, presented at the August 15, 2023 regular Board meeting.

Rationale
The effort grew from the strategic plan refresh, in which stakeholders called for stronger student voice, and from the Board's request for a clearer, student-centered measure of "success." It cites education author Tony Wagner on the value of seeking input from the students most affected by district policy.

Data sample
- Parents: a 3-question open-ended survey; 308 completed responses; 60+ pages of transcripts; 24,000+ words; 94% positive and constructive remarks.
- Principals: a 45-minute discussion at an all-principals K-12 meeting.
- Students: 30-minute discussions across 16 classrooms (four high schools, three middle schools, four elementary schools, one preschool); 320+ students.

Core questions
Participants were asked what the district does best today, which hard and soft skills matter most before graduation, and what "secret sauce" should mark a Troy graduate as an adult.

Key finding
Near-perfect overlap in stated priorities among students, parents, and principals, in tight alignment with the District Strategic Plan pillars.

The 12 traits
Visionary; Connected; Kind, Compassionate, and Inclusive; Joyous about Discovery; Eager for Challenge; Tenacious; Intellectual "crackerjack"; Adaptable; Self-starter; Good Team Player; Organized; and Confident Communicator. The deck also notes high schoolers' sense of disconnect between classroom learning and career planning, and that students at the smaller TCCHS and IAE cited adult engagement as central to their success.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A summary presentation delivered to the Troy School District Board of Education at its August 15, 2023 regular meeting, documenting the data-gathering phase of the "Portrait of a Troy Graduate" initiative. The stated rationale draws on education expert Tony Wagner's emphasis on seeking input from the stakeholders most influenced by district policy—students—and responds to two signals: feedback during the strategic plan refresh calling for stronger student voice, and the Board's repeated request for a clearer, student-perspective measure of "success" in executing the strategic plan. The purpose was to identify the traits the district should expect to see in its graduates if it is delivering on its promise of a world-class education.

The data sample spanned three stakeholder groups. Parents completed a three-question open-ended survey, yielding 308 completed surveys, more than 60 pages of transcripts, over 24,000 words, and 94% positive and constructive remarks. Principals participated in a 45-minute discussion at an all-principals K-12 meeting. Students took part in 30-minute discussions across 16 classrooms—four high schools, three middle schools, four elementary schools, and one preschool—involving more than 320 students.

The core question progression asked: what is the best of what the district is doing to date; what are the most critical hard and soft skills to foster before students leave; and, as an adult, what is the "secret sauce" that should mark a Troy graduate. The presentation reported near-perfect consensus, describing an almost perfect overlap in stated priorities among students, parents, and principals, in tight alignment with the District Strategic Plan pillars. It framed this as evidence that either district strategy matches parent and student ideals, the district has effectively communicated the value of the pillars, or both. A definition is quoted from a second grader named Leonard, who told a facilitator named Karl that "a portrait is two things: it's a picture of you and it's like the best parts of you."

The exercise produced 12 traits of a TSD graduate: Visionary; Connected; Kind, Compassionate, and Inclusive; Joyous about Discovery; Eager for Challenge; Tenacious; Intellectual "crackerjack"; Adaptable; Self-starter; Good Team Player; Organized; and Confident Communicator. The deck elaborates several. "Visionary" describes a student who can confidently connect formal education and school experiences to the real world and their own future; it notes high schoolers often felt a disconnect between classroom work and a specific degree program or career, and complained that career planning was disconnected from academics. "Connected" describes someone who builds meaningful relationships with peers and adults; high schoolers held up teacher relationships as one of the most important elements of their success, and in the district's two larger high schools felt caring teachers were "more the exception than the rule," while students at the smaller TCCHS and IAE identified adult emotional investment as a primary reason for their success. "Kind, Compassionate, and Inclusive" describes intrinsically treating others with kindness, respect, and fairness, with emphasis on recognizing and valuing differences in an increasingly multicultural world. "Joyous about Discovery" describes an enthusiastic, lifelong learner curious about the world (the extracted text truncates at this trait). The document is a PowerPoint slide deck.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Board presentation from September 19, 2023 recapping Troy School District's summer 2023 professional learning and student summer-school programs under the 'OneTroy' banner. Staff development included the TSD Literacy Project (over 80 teachers, K-2 through 9-10), a seventh-year Preschool Literacy & Math Institute (50 staff), mathematics institutes, principal retreats tied to bond engagement, and new-teacher orientation. Student programs included the Troy Summer Learning Lab (112 students entering grades 6-8, 21 staff mentors, Stanford design-thinking model), Title I offerings such as Morse Summer Nights and Herd of Words, and multilingual-learner programs serving roughly 184 students across Morse, Troy Union, and Boulan.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
September 19, 2023 Board of Education presentation, 'Summer Professional Learning and Summer School Update,' summarizing OneTroy summer 2023 staff development and student programs.

Staff professional learning
- TSD Literacy Project: over 80 teachers across K-2, 3-5, 6-8, and 9-10; sustaining the Workshop Method PreK-10 and responsive teaching.
- Preschool Literacy & Math Institute: 50 teachers and assistants; seventh year of preschool summer learning.
- Mathematics Institutes: Math Recovery, Bridges, and Middle School institutes.
- Principal Retreats & Admin Kick-Off: reviewing Mission, Vision, Values, and Thematic Goals, plus bond-engagement topics (furniture, playgrounds, Smith Design).
- New Teacher Orientation: four-day PD with each department, a district tour, and mentor time.

Student summer programs
- Troy Summer Learning Lab: free program for students entering grades 6-8; Stanford design-thinking process; 112 students from all four middle schools; 21 TSD staff mentors/teachers.
- Title I opportunities: Morse Summer Nights / Morse Reads and 'Morse to You' (books delivered to a local mobile-home park), virtual Summer Book Clubs for 3rd-5th graders below grade level, Herd of Words writing and art camp (rising grades 1-5), Title I Summer School (grades K-4, new Bridges math), and Morse Media Center summer reading.
- Multilingual learners: Morse (96 students) and Troy Union (72) for grades K-7; Boulan (16) for grades 8-12, with Friday field trips; transportation provided.

Purpose
Inform the Board of summer programming reach, staffing, and instructional design.

Its stated objective under 'Building Capacity' is to provide professional learning opportunities for staff, community, and students throughout 'OneTroy.'

Summer staff professional learning: The 'OneTroy Summer Learning' offerings included Summer Curriculum Development, an Administrative Kick-Off Meeting, a Teaching and Learning Team Retreat, a Cabinet Retreat, Literacy & Mathematics work, Pre-K Literacy & Math, Troy Institutes K-12, and New Teacher Orientation. The TSD Literacy Project involved over 80 teachers spanning grade bands K-2, 3-5, 6-8, and 9-10, focused on sustaining the Workshop Method PreK-10 and responsive teaching. The Preschool Literacy & Math Institute drew 50 staff members (teachers and assistants) and marked the seventh year of summer learning for preschool staff. Mathematics offerings comprised a Math Recovery Institute, a Bridges Institute, and a Middle School Institute. Principal Retreats and the Admin Kick-Off asked leaders to reflect on the current state and next steps to sustain vision work, review the district's Mission, Vision, Values, and Thematic Goals, and hold level-specific meetings for bond engagement covering furniture, playgrounds, and 'Smith Design.' New Teacher Orientation was a four-day professional development with each department, a tour of the district, and time with mentor teachers, followed by an August staff welcome-back.

Student summer programs: The presentation emphasized providing access to all students in need using a flexible delivery model and grant funding when possible, with district-level teams working alongside building teams. The Troy Summer Learning Lab was a free program for students entering grades 6-8 focused on Deep Learning, using the Stanford design-thinking process so students could undertake a project of their own choosing; it began with two weeks of immersion featuring guest speakers and field trips and moved through defining problems, ideating, and prototyping a solution. It served 112 students from all four district middle schools with 21 TSD staff serving as mentors and teachers.

Title I Summer Opportunities included: Morse Summer Nights / Morse Reads, a bi-weekly program keeping families engaged with literacy and math, including a 'Morse to You' outreach that brought a collection of books and projects to a local mobile-home park for students who could not get to the school; Summer Book Clubs, two virtual sessions (Tuesday-Thursday) for 3rd-5th graders reading below grade level, each given five leveled books to read together on TEAMS; the Herd of Words Writing and Art Camp for rising grades 1-5, teaching revision through both writing journals and painting; Title I Summer School for grades K-4 performing at or below grade level in math, reading, or writing, incorporating the new Bridges math curriculum plus media and physical-education enrichment; and the Morse Media Center summer reading hour open after each summer-school session.

Summer Programs for Multilingual Learners: Morse and Troy Union hosted grades K-7 - Morse served 96 students and Troy Union served 72, each running 3 hours a day, 3 days a week, for 5 weeks with TSD/EDUStaff certified teachers and assistants; students who received Intensive ELD instruction during 2022-23 were invited to build English proficiency through content-area topics and leveled readers, with transportation provided. Boulan hosted grades 8-12, serving 16 students over 4 hours a day, 4 days a week, for 5 weeks plus Friday field trips; multilingual learners entering Beginner or Intermediate ELD English courses were invited to take the class for an English elective credit or for no credit, with Friday trips to the Detroit Institute of Arts, Greenfield Village, the Detroit Zoo, Stony Creek Metropark, and the Troy Public Library.

What it is
RECOGNITION item 2.E: a suggested resolution / proclamation recognizing September 2023 as National Suicide Prevention Month, presented at the Troy School District Board of Education meeting of September 19, 2023. Recommended action is acceptance of the resolution.

Origin
The Oakland Community Health Network (OCHN) asked school boards throughout Oakland County to partner with it by approving this proclamation at their September board meetings.

Key facts cited
- World Suicide Prevention Day is observed each year on September 10.
- Per the CDC, more than 48,000 people die by suicide each year.
- Suicide is the second leading cause of death for people ages 10 to 34, fourth for ages 35 to 54, and eighth for ages 55 to 64.
- Organizations named: National Alliance on Mental Illness (NAMI) and the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline, 988.
- OCHN is committed to being a 'Zero Suicide' organization.

Resolution
'NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED' that OCHN recognizes September 2023 as National Suicide Prevention Month and calls upon individuals, government agencies, institutions, businesses, faith-based organizations, and schools to increase awareness of suicide prevention and accessible crisis services. Includes Moved by / Supported by lines and YES/NO tallies for the vote.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Agenda item 2.E, dated 09.20.23, is a RECOGNITION item presenting a suggested resolution to recognize September 2023 as National Suicide Prevention Month at the Troy School District Board of Education meeting of September 19, 2023. The item explains that the Oakland Community Health Network (OCHN) asked school boards throughout Oakland County to partner with it by approving such a proclamation at their September board meetings. The recommended action is acceptance of the resolution, which includes 'Moved by' and 'Supported by' lines and YES/NO tallies for recording the vote.

The resolution's WHEREAS clauses state: September is known as National Suicide Prevention Month, intended to raise awareness of suicide prevention resources in the community; World Suicide Prevention Day is observed each year on September 10; suicidal thoughts can affect anyone regardless of age, gender, race, orientation, income level, religion, or background; according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), each year more than 48,000 people died by suicide; suicide is the second leading cause of death for people 10 to 34 years of age, the fourth leading cause among people 35 to 54, and the eighth leading cause among people 55 to 64; organizations like the National Alliance on Mental Illness (NAMI) and the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline, 988, work to help individuals in crisis and provide resources on this stigmatized topic; every member of the community should understand that we all need occasional reminders that we are all silently fighting our own battles; and OCHN is committed to being a Zero Suicide organization and to cultivating a network of providers engaged in the Zero Suicide philosophy.

The operative clause reads: 'NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that, Oakland Community Health Network hereby recognizes September 2023 as National Suicide Prevention Month.' OCHN calls upon individuals, government agencies, public and private institutions, businesses, faith-based organizations, and schools to recommit to increasing awareness and understanding of suicide prevention and the need for appropriate and accessible services to assist individuals in crisis. The document is a partnership proclamation adopted at the local board level; its substantive content is the recognition and the supporting public-health statistics rather than any budgetary or contractual action.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This is the 2023-2024 Course Description Book for Troy College and Career High School (TCCHS), presented as consent-agenda item 5.E for the Troy School District Board of Education meeting of September 19, 2023. The cover identifies Dr. Richard Machesky as Superintendent of Schools.

The book opens with the Troy School District Policy of Nondiscrimination (revised August 2023), addressed to students, parents, and citizens. It recites Title IX of the Educational Amendments of 1972 and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 together with the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), stating that the district does not discriminate on the basis of sex or handicap in admission, access, treatment, or employment, and that it maintains a grievance procedure for prompt and equitable resolution of complaints. It names Jordan M. Harris, J.D., Assistant Superintendent of Employee Services, as Title IX and Section 504/ADA Coordinator for employment and personnel matters, and designates the District's Director of Special Education as the Section 504/ADA Coordinator for handicapped and suspected handicapped students. Questions are directed to John Pagel, Assistant Superintendent of Employee Services, at Troy School District, 4400 Livernois Road, Troy, MI 48098-4799, (248) 823-4000.

TCCHS is led by Principal Mrs. Angela Milanov and located at 1522 East Big Beaver Road, Troy, MI 48083, phone 248.823.5156. Graduation requirements state that all TCCHS students must earn 19.5 credits to be eligible for a Troy School District high school diploma, while students seeking a diploma from Troy High School or Athens High School must meet the 22.5-credit requirement outlined in the THS & AHS course description book. In alignment with alternative education needs, TCCHS allows students with demonstrated need to deviate from the 19.5-credit requirement after meeting with a counselor or administrator. All TCCHS students must complete 8 semesters / 4 years of high school and the 18 credits required by the Michigan Department of Education.

Graduation Requirement Flexibility Options (updated 9.2015, citing MCL 380.1278a and MCL 380.1278b) include: a Personal Curriculum allowing additional credits in some core academic areas in lieu of others; physical education credit earned through athletics, extra-curricular activities, or a counselor-approved PE class; a World Language requirement of 2.0 credits, with flexibility for non-English heritage language proficiency, international study and residence, or substitution of Career & Technical Education or Visual & Performing or Applied Arts credits; and Career & Technical Education (CTE) Program Completion, whereby students completing a CTE program of study can exchange those credits on a 1:1 basis for required science or world language credits or satisfy the Algebra 2 requirement through a CTE program with embedded Algebra 2 content. The catalog then begins its course listings; a sample CTE course, Woodworking Design & Fabrication 1 (one-half credit per semester, no prerequisite, satisfying one credit of the math-related graduation requirement in grade 12), introduces students to designing, drawing, and manufacturing projects using CAD software, hand and power tools, power machines, and automation including CNC and 3D printing, followed by Woodworking Design & Fabrication 2. The extracted text is truncated and shows some OCR duplication.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
An external auditor's board presentation summarizing the Troy School District's audited financial results for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2023, delivered at the October 3, 2023 board workshop.

Audit highlights: the district received an unmodified (clean) opinion on its 2023 financial-statement audit and an unmodified opinion on its 2023 federal program audit with no findings or questioned costs. The presentation notes Bond and Sinking Fund compliance, Budgeting Act compliance, a non-recurring 147(c)(2) allocation, receipt of the ASBO Certificate of Excellence in Financial Reporting for 2022, and non-recurring revenue sources including federal ESSER and federal childcare grants.

COVID-19 relief funding: total allocated was $28,411 thousand (about $28.4 million) with $24,580 thousand (about $24.6 million) expended to date. Components (allocated) include CRF $6,501K, ESSER I $246K, ESSER II $1,675K, ESSER II Equalization (State) $5,036K, ESSER III $1,895K, ESSER III Equalization $12,385K (of which $8,589K expended), GEER $22K, GEER II $53K, and ARP-IDEA $598K.

Governmental funds (June 30, 2023): the General Fund had revenue of $189,049,577 and expenditures of $189,410,093, an excess of expenditures over revenue of $360,516. The 2023 Capital Projects Fund had revenue of $2,921,374 and expenditures of $4,587,802; with $171,370,000 face value of debt issued and an $18,977,094 premium ($190,347,094 total other financing sources), its fund balance grew to $188,680,666. Total Nonmajor Funds had revenue of $43,660,071 and expenditures of $44,945,845, ending at $16,387,475 (from $17,673,249).

General Fund revenue of $189,049,577 breaks down as State source $127,900,185 (68%), Local $40,849,017 (21%), Interdistrict $11,080,715 (6%), and Federal $9,219,660 (5%). A foundation view shows State Portion of Foundation Allowance $84,489,876 (45%), Other State and Local $57,332,614 (30%), Property Taxes $38,007,427 (20%), and Federal $9,219,660 (5%). General Fund expenditures of $189,410,093 by object are Salaries and Employee Benefits $155,555,983 (82%), Purchased Services $24,852,659 (13%), Supplies $6,844,574 (4%), and Other Expenses $2,156,877 (1%). By function, Direct Instruction was 65.96% (versus an Oakland County FY22 average of 60.29%), Indirect Instruction 13.61%, Operations and Maintenance 7.34%, School Administration 5.52%, Pupil Transportation 2.18%, Central Services 1.97%, General Administration and Business Services 1.78%, Athletics 1.27%, Debt Service 0.25%, and Community Services 0.12%.

Enrollment and foundation: 2023-24 membership was 12,282 pupils with a foundation allowance of $10,332, up from 12,419 pupils and $9,874 in 2022-23; a slide labeled "Super Blend" traces membership and allowance back to 2008-09 (12,177 pupils, $9,275). In a 2022-23 comparison of Oakland County foundation revenue per pupil, Troy's $9,874 ranked mid-pack, below Bloomfield Hills ($12,985), Birmingham ($12,905), Southfield ($11,952), Lamphere ($11,410), and Farmington ($11,026), and above West Bloomfield, Royal Oak, Novi, Walled Lake, Rochester, Waterford, and Huron Valley.

Fund balance: the General Fund balance ended the year at $32,620,321, down from $32,980,837, equal to 17.22% of expenditures, or about 9.0 weeks (63 days) of operations. Over ten years the balance rose from $21,380,015 (FY2014) to a peak of $32,980,837 (FY2022), with the fund-balance-to-expenditure ratio ranging from roughly 15% to a high of 19.88% in FY2021.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Draft 'Report to the Board of Education' prepared by the external audit firm for Troy School District (the 'School District') covering the audit of the district's basic financial statements as of and for the year ended June 30, 2023. The letter is dated October 3, 2023 and marked DRAFT throughout. It transmits the auditor's required communications and points to three report sections: Results of the Audit (pages 3-6), Other Recommendations and Observations (pages 7-8), and Informational Items (pages 9-19).

The firm thanks Mr. Rick West, Ms. Kandice Moynihan, and the entire business office for their assistance and preparedness during the audit, noting that audit preparation is carried out in addition to staff's normal daily activities.

Auditor responsibility: As stated in the engagement letter dated May 31, 2023, the auditor's responsibility is to express an opinion on whether management's financial statements are fairly presented, in all material respects, in conformity with U.S. generally accepted accounting principles. The audit is planned and performed to obtain reasonable, but not absolute, assurance that the statements are free of material misstatement, and does not relieve management or the board of their responsibilities. Internal control was considered solely to design audit procedures, not to opine on the effectiveness of internal control.

Government Auditing Standards: The audit was also conducted in accordance with Government Auditing Standards issued by the Comptroller General of the United States, obligating the auditor to communicate certain matters including compliance with provisions of laws, regulations, contracts, and grant agreements; instances of error or fraud; illegal acts applicable to government agencies; and significant deficiencies in internal control. A separate letter dated October 3, 2023 addresses the auditor's consideration of internal control over financial reporting and tests of compliance.

Scope and timing: The audit was performed according to the scope and timing previously communicated at the planning meeting on August 4, 2023.

Significant audit findings and qualitative aspects: Management is responsible for selecting appropriate accounting policies, which are described in Note 2 to the financial statements. No new accounting policies were adopted and the application of existing policies was not changed during 2023. The auditor noted no transactions lacking authoritative guidance or consensus and no significant transactions recognized in a different period than when they occurred. Accounting estimates are described as an integral part of the statements, based on management's knowledge and assumptions about future events; the most sensitive estimates affecting the financial statements were the School District's share of the MPSERS net liabilities for the pension and other postemployment benefit (OPEB) plans, which are particularly sensitive because of their significance and the possibility that future events may differ significantly from expectations.

The document is a draft presented to the Board of Education Workshop on October 3, 2023, accompanying the district's draft Annual Comprehensive Financial Report and draft Single Audit for the same fiscal year. (The extracted text ends mid-sentence within the discussion of sensitive estimates.)

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Crosswalk document titled 'How this relates to Classroom: NPDL/TSD' that aligns Troy School District's Portrait of a Learner framework with the New Pedagogies for Deep Learning (NPDL) model. It is organized around student-voice 'As a student I will...' competency descriptors and maps six competencies to twelve 'Idea Traits.'

The six competencies, each with its NPDL descriptors and the paired TSD student trait(s):
- CHARACTER (Tenacious & Self Starter): a proactive stance toward life and learning to learn; grit, tenacity, perseverance, and resilience; empathy, compassion, and integrity in action - deep learning armed with essential character traits and making learning an integral part of living.
- COMMUNICATION (Confident Communicator & Organized): communication designed for audience and impact; a message that advocates a purpose and makes an impact; reflection to improve communication; voice and identity expressed to advance humanity - communicating effectively with a variety of styles, modes, and digital tools tailored for a range of audiences.
- CITIZENSHIP (Kind, Compassionate, Inclusive): a global perspective; commitment to human equity and well-being through empathy and compassion for diverse values and worldviews; genuine interest in human and environmental sustainability; solving ambiguous, complex real-world problems to benefit citizens.
- CREATIVITY (Joyous About Discovery & Adaptable): economic and social entrepreneurialism; asking the right inquiry questions; pursuing and expressing novel ideas and solutions; leadership to turn ideas into action - having an 'entrepreneurial eye' for opportunities.
- COLLABORATION (Connected & Good Team Player): working interdependently as a team; interpersonal and team-related skills; social, emotional, and intercultural skills; managing team dynamics and challenges.
- CRITICAL THINKING (Visionary, Eager for Challenge & Intellectual): evaluating information and arguments; making connections and identifying patterns; meaningful knowledge construction; experimenting, reflecting, and taking action on ideas in the real world.

The twelve Idea Traits are each defined and tagged to a pillar color:
- Visionary (GREEN): confidently connects formal education and student experiences to the real world and their own immediate and long-term future.
- Connected (RED): has built meaningful relationships with peers and adults and understands the deep value in those connections.
- Kind, Compassionate, Inclusive (RED): intrinsically treats others with kindness, respect, and fairness.
- Joyous About Discovery (BLUE): an enthusiastic, curious lifelong learner eager to explore new topics and ventures.
- Eager for Challenge (BLUE): excited to tackle any challenge and unafraid of 'Big Hairy Audacious Goals' or problems.
- Tenacious (BLUE): marked by grit and adept in situations that require productive struggle.
- Intellectual (BLUE): an adept 'synthesizer' who draws meaningful conclusions from data, research, and people.
- Adaptable (BLUE): flexible in incorporating new information and willing to pivot when beneficial.
- Self-Starter (GOLD): confident and willing to tackle deep, complex projects with little assistance.
- Good Team Player (GOLD): can lead or contribute in a group, understanding interpersonal dynamics and intellectual humility.
- Organized (GOLD): top-notch organization, time-management, and project-management skills.
- Confident Communicator (GOLD): easily conveys ideas, information, and perspective via conversation, writing, and interactive media.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
A 'Learning Progressions - Character' rubric written in student-friendly, first-person language describing how a learner grows across the Character competency. Sourced from New Pedagogies for Deep Learning (NPDL) and used in Troy School District's deep-learning / Portrait of a Learner framework.

Progression levels
Five stages across each dimension: Limited Evidence, Emerging, Developing, Accelerating, and Proficient.

Dimensions
- Proactive stance toward life and learning to deep learn (from 'I am not clear about what I need to learn and why' up to creating meaningful, self-directed learning and solutions that impact the world).
- Grit, tenacity, perseverance, and resilience (from giving up when challenged to persevering through major setbacks and helping others do the same).
- Empathy, compassion, and integrity (from uncertainty about others' feelings to consistently modeling compassion, empathy, and integrity even when inconvenient).
- Using technology for learning / leveraging digital (from using digital without seeing its value to effortlessly using it and supporting others' learning).

Attribution
Copyright 2019 Education in Motion (New Pedagogies for Deep Learning); reproduction authorized for educational use by purchasers.

Purpose
Give students a common, self-assessable language for growth in Character; a companion to the district's Character self-assessment form. Presented at the October 3, 2023 Board of Education Workshop.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
'Learning Progressions - Character | Student-Friendly Deep Learning Progression,' a rubric that describes, in first-person 'I' statements, how a learner develops across the Character competency. It is part of Troy School District's deep-learning / Portrait of a Learner materials and is drawn from New Pedagogies for Deep Learning (NPDL); the footer credits 'Copyright (c) 2019 by Education in Motion (New Pedagogies for Deep Learning),' with reproduction authorized for educational use by educators and local school sites that have purchased the book. It was presented at the October 3, 2023 Board of Education Workshop.

The progression is framed by the Character definition: 'Learning to deep learn, to keep trying, to have integrity, empathy, and compassion, and to always be a learner.' Each dimension is described across five developmental levels: Limited Evidence, Emerging, Developing, Accelerating, and Proficient.

Proactive stance toward life and learning to deep learn: At Limited Evidence the student is 'not clear about what I need to learn and why,' can complete teacher-prepared tasks but needs help to reflect, and does not yet find learning positive. Through Emerging and Developing, the student learns to identify what they know and need to learn, chooses topics and designs projects, and uses peer and teacher feedback to improve. At Accelerating and Proficient, the student understands what they need to learn and how to learn it, reflects on progress, finds and creates their own learning opportunities, continually builds knowledge and skills, and 'creates meaningful solutions that impact my life and the world,' actively seeking feedback and balancing work with play.

Grit, tenacity, perseverance, and resilience: The lowest level describes a student who 'usually give[s] up when I face an unexpected challenge' and needs a lot of support with setbacks. Higher levels describe starting to persevere with encouragement, dealing with small and medium challenges by pausing, reflecting, adapting, and finding new solutions, and ultimately persevering through the most challenging tasks and major setbacks, understanding why the character qualities matter, and helping others do the same.

Empathy, compassion, and integrity: Levels move from being 'not sure about what other people might feel' to beginning to put oneself in others' shoes, imagining how others experience the world, wanting to develop empathy and courage to do the right thing, and finally regularly modeling compassion, empathy, and integrity 'even when no one notices or when it is inconvenient,' valuing virtues such as sincerity, fairness, trustworthiness, and bravery.

Using technology for learning (leveraging digital): Progresses from using digital tools without seeing how they support learning, to using them to develop traits like empathy, compassion, and grit, to knowing and explaining how digital helps learning, to effortlessly using technology throughout learning and using it to support others by encouraging them and providing feedback.

The rubric is a companion to the district's blank Character student self-assessment form and gives students a shared, self-assessable vocabulary for growth in the Character competency.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose: A recognition resolution (agenda 2.D.) presented at the October 17, 2023 regular meeting under which the Troy School District Board of Education commemorates October 2023 as Learning Disabilities Month in Michigan, joining Governor Gretchen Whitmer. The preamble notes that national associations for a number of different learning differences have each declared October as an awareness month, including associations for Dyslexia, Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder, and Down Syndrome, and that the U.S. Department of Education has declared October as Learning Disabilities / Dyslexia / Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder / Down Syndrome Awareness Month, while in Michigan Governor Whitmer has provided a more encompassing definition and declared October as Learning Disabilities Month. The resolution's WHEREAS clauses state that the term learning disabilities refers to differences in how our brains work, which may affect the acquisition, organization, retention, understanding, or use of verbal or nonverbal information; that learning disabilities range in severity and may impact oral language, reading, written language, and mathematics; that 1 in 5 individuals have a learning disability; that learning disabilities may co-exist with other disabilities and can affect individuals regardless of race, gender, sexual orientation, or other intersecting factors; that individuals with learning disabilities may face discrimination or marginalization; that every person has strengths and learning disabilities should not keep individuals from realizing their full potential in school, at work or home, or in their families and communities; that specialized assessments and interventions across home, school, community, and workplace settings can significantly enhance quality of life; and that appropriate supports and services enable individuals with learning disabilities to achieve their goals and participate fully in society. The operative clause states that the Troy School District Board of Education joins Governor Gretchen Whitmer in commemorating October 2023 as Learning Disabilities Month in Michigan. The recommended action is acceptance of the resolution, with blank lines for the mover, supporter, and YES/NO votes; no vote outcome is recorded on this copy.

Expenditures. By object: salaries and employee benefits $155,555,983 (82%), purchased services $24,852,659 (13%), supplies $6,844,574 (4%), and other expenses $2,156,877 (1%). By function: direct instruction 65.96%, indirect instruction 13.61%, operations and maintenance 7.34%, school administration 5.52%, pupil transportation 2.18%, central services 1.97%, general administration and business services 1.78%, athletics 1.27%, debt service 0.25%, and community services 0.12%. Enrollment and foundation allowance. The 2023-2024 foundation allowance is $10,332 with a student population of 12,282, up from $9,874 and 12,419 in 2022-2023; a footnote references 2008-2009 as the final year of 20j funding at $248.18 per pupil and a "Super Blend." https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
The Troy School District Annual Comprehensive Financial Report (ACFR) for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2023, presented to the Board of Education on October 17, 2023 as agenda item 8.B. The report was prepared by the school district's Department of Business Services and covers all activities under the control of the Board of Education. The cover identifies the Administration Building at 4400 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098, phone (248) 823-4000, fax (248) 823-4013.

Contents. The document is organized into the standard ACFR sections. The Introductory Section (pages i-xiv) contains the letter of transmittal, members of the Board of Education and administration, an organization chart, and the Association of School Business Officials International (ASBO) Certificate of Excellence. The Financial Section contains the independent auditor's report (pages 1-3), management's discussion and analysis (pages 4-10), the basic financial statements, and notes (pages 19-38). The basic financial statements comprise government-wide statements (Statement of Net Position; Statement of Activities), governmental fund statements (balance sheet; statement of revenue, expenditures, and changes in fund balances, with reconciliations), and fiduciary fund statements. Required Supplementary Information (pages 39-46) includes a General Fund budgetary comparison schedule and schedules of the district's proportionate share of the net pension liability and net OPEB liability with related contribution schedules. Other Supplementary Information includes combining statements for nonmajor governmental funds, a schedule of bonded indebtedness (pages 52-53), and budgetary comparison schedules. The Statistical Section (pages 56-79) presents financial-trend information (net position by component, changes in governmental net position, fund balances), revenue-capacity information (taxable and actual value of property, direct and overlapping property tax rates, principal property taxpayers, property tax levies and collections), debt-capacity information (ratios of general bonded debt outstanding, direct and overlapping debt, legal debt margin), demographic and economic statistics, principal employers, and operating information including full-time equivalent employees and capital assets. The Federal Awards Supplemental Information is issued under separate cover.

Transmittal letter. Dated October 3, 2023 and addressed to the citizens of Troy and the Board members, the letter states that responsibility for the accuracy, completeness, and fairness of the presentation rests with the school district, and that the data is believed accurate in all material respects. It affirms that the Troy School District is an independent reporting entity meeting the criteria established by the Governmental Accounting Standards Board, that all funds of the school district are included, and that the district does not have component units. The financial section reports separately the government-wide activities, the governmental fund types, and the fiduciary fund type administered by the board. The letter is signed by Rick West, Deputy Superintendent, and Kandice Moynihan, Director of Finance (contact rwest@troy.k12.mi.us), and is intended to complement the management's discussion and analysis, with which it should be read.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
An external auditor's "Report to the Board of Education" for the Troy School District covering the year ended June 30, 2023, presented with agenda item 8.B. and dated October 3, 2023. Commonly called a management letter, it accompanies the audit report and conveys required governance communications, a summary of unrecorded possible adjustments, and other recommendations, observations, and informational items.

Structure. The report is organized into Results of the Audit (pages 1-4), Other Recommendations and Observations (pages 5-6), and Informational Items (pages 7-16). The auditor thanks Mr. Rick West, Ms. Kandice Moynihan, and the entire business office for their assistance and preparedness during the audit, noting that audit preparation is carried out in addition to staff's normal daily activities.

Auditor responsibility. The letter states that the auditor audited the financial statements of the School District as of and for the year ended June 30, 2023 and issued a report dated October 3, 2023. Under U.S. generally accepted auditing standards, and as set out in the engagement letter dated May 31, 2023, the auditor's responsibility is to express an opinion about whether the financial statements prepared by management with the Board's oversight are fairly presented, in all material respects, in conformity with U.S. generally accepted accounting principles; the audit provides reasonable but not absolute assurance and does not relieve management or the Board of their responsibilities. As part of the audit the auditor considered the district's internal control solely to design audit procedures, not to opine on its effectiveness. The audit was also conducted in accordance with Government Auditing Standards issued by the Comptroller General of the United States, under which the auditor is obligated to communicate matters such as noncompliance with laws, regulations, contracts, and grant agreements, instances of error or fraud, illegal acts, and significant internal-control deficiencies; a separate letter dated October 3, 2023 addresses internal control over financial reporting and compliance testing.

Scope and timing. The audit was performed according to the planned scope and timing previously communicated, following a planning-matters meeting on August 4, 2023.

Significant audit findings. The auditor reports that management is responsible for selecting and using appropriate accounting policies (described in Note 2 to the financial statements), that no new accounting policies were adopted, and that the application of existing policies was not changed during 2023. No transactions were noted for which there is a lack of authoritative guidance or consensus, and no significant transactions were recognized in a different period than when they occurred. The most sensitive accounting estimates affecting the financial statements were the School District's share of the MPSERS net liabilities for the pension and other postemployment benefit (OPEB) plans recorded on the government-wide statements, related to GASB Statement Nos. 68 and 75, respectively. Regarding internal control over financial reporting, the auditor did not identify any deficiencies considered to be material weaknesses, while cautioning that unidentified material weaknesses or significant deficiencies may exist.

The Troy School District Federal Awards Supplemental Information for the year ended June 30, 2023, presented with agenda item 8.B. This is the district's "single audit" reporting package prepared under the federal Uniform Guidance, issued as a companion to the basic financial statements.

Contents. The package includes the independent auditor's report on the Schedule of Expenditures of Federal Awards required by the Uniform Guidance (page 1); the report on internal control over financial reporting and on compliance and other matters based on an audit of financial statements performed in accordance with Government Auditing Standards (pages 2-3); the report on compliance for each major federal program and on internal control over compliance required by the Uniform Guidance (pages 4-6); the Schedule of Expenditures of Federal Awards (pages 7-10); a reconciliation of basic financial-statement federal revenue with the schedule of expenditures of federal awards (page 11); notes to the schedule (page 12); and the Schedule of Findings and Questioned Costs (page 13).

Auditor's opinion on the schedule. The auditor states that it audited the financial statements of the governmental activities, each major fund, and the aggregate remaining fund information of the School District as of and for the year ended June 30, 2023, and issued a report dated October 3, 2023 containing unmodified opinions. The accompanying schedule of expenditures of federal awards and reconciliation are presented for purposes of additional analysis as required by the Uniform Guidance and are not a required part of the basic financial statements. That information was subjected to the auditing procedures applied in the audit and, in the auditor's opinion, is fairly stated in all material respects in relation to the financial statements as a whole.

Internal control and compliance. In planning and performing the audit, the auditor considered the School District's internal control over financial reporting to design appropriate audit procedures, not to express an opinion on the effectiveness of internal control. The auditor states that this consideration was for a limited purpose and was not designed to identify all deficiencies that might be material weaknesses or significant deficiencies. During the audit the auditor did not identify any deficiencies in internal control that it considers to be material weaknesses, while noting that material weaknesses or significant deficiencies may exist that were not identified. The report defines, in standard terms, a deficiency in internal control and a material weakness. The extracted text does not include the dollar figures from the Schedule of Expenditures of Federal Awards or the specific contents of the Schedule of Findings and Questioned Costs.

Budget figures are drawn from the approved budget adopted June 13, 2023.

General Fund. The approved revenue budget is $187,031,432, comprising Local Sources $43,788,278, State Sources $123,125,300, Federal Sources $7,980,072, and Interdistrict Sources $12,137,782; two-month actual revenue is $7,593,512 (Local $7,406,575, Federal $125,465, Interdistrict $61,472, with no state aid yet received). The approved expenditure budget is $185,981,740; two-month actual expenditures are $8,050,728. On the expenditure side, budgeted Total Instruction is $121,536,100 (Basic Programs $90,145,544, Added Needs $30,445,199, Adult Education $945,357) with $1,594,289 spent to date, and budgeted Total Support Services is $63,765,159 (including Operations $14,159,333, Pupil $14,522,814, Instructional Staff $11,599,560, School Administration $9,708,700, Pupil Transportation $4,330,166, Central Services $3,781,018) with $6,448,054 spent to date. Community Services is budgeted at $204,481 and Debt Service at $476,000. The budget projects revenues over expenditures of $1,049,692, while the two-month actuals show revenues under expenditures of $(457,216), typical early in a fiscal year before state aid payments begin.

Consolidated Debt Service Funds. Budgeted revenue is $30,715,000 (Local $30,440,000, State $275,000) against budgeted expenditures of $30,853,519 (Principal $18,745,000, Interest $12,105,019, Other $3,500), a budgeted shortfall of $(138,519); two-month actuals are $5,109,665 in revenue (mostly local property taxes) and only $350 in expenditures, since debt payments occur later in the year.

Special Revenue Funds. The Food Service Fund (520) has budgeted revenue of $6,380,500 and expenditures of $5,678,545 (budgeted surplus $701,955); two-month actuals are $123,104 revenue and $168,600 expenditures, a $(45,496) deficit. The Troy Career Center Fund (529) has a balanced budget of $2,773,800 in both revenue and expenditures, with two-month actuals of $376,142 each and zero net. The Community Service Fund (530) has budgeted revenue of $2,013,000 and expenditures of $1,838,574 (surplus $174,426); actuals are $296,270 revenue and $269,756 expenditures, a $26,514 surplus. The Troy Preschool Fund (531) has budgeted revenue of $3,795,614 and expenditures of $3,310,400 (surplus $485,214); actuals are $302,644 revenue and $196,751 expenditures, a $105,893 surplus. A further fund, its heading truncated in the extracted text, shows budgeted Local Sources revenue of $225,000 with $15,779 received.

Overall, the statement gives the Board an early-year, budget-to-actual snapshot across the General Fund and the district's debt-service and special-revenue funds; the small percentages of budget realized reflect that only two of twelve months had elapsed and that major state-aid and debt-service transactions occur later in the year.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A November 2023 board workshop presentation on Troy School District student assessment data, emphasizing consistent measures over time. It reviews the SAT Suite (SAT 11, PSAT 8) and M-STEP grades 3-7 alongside benchmarking tools (Fountas & Pinnell, CommonLit, and NWEA Math) and exit measures such as AP results and graduation rate. The deck breaks SAT and PSAT results into math subcategories (Heart of Algebra, Passport to Advanced Math, Problem Solving and Data Analysis) and reading/writing subcategories, and announces NWEA's winter rollout to replace district-created math benchmarks under a new K-8 curriculum with Illustrative Math.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
A Student Assessment Data board workshop deck presented in November 2023, laying out the district's approach to measuring achievement with consistent instruments over time.

Assessment framework
- Standardized: SAT Suite of Assessments, SAT 11 (Scholastic Aptitude Test), PSAT 8, and M-STEP grades 3-7
- Instructional/benchmarking: Fountas & Pinnell (ELA K-5), CommonLit (ELA 6-12), NWEA Math (grade 6-Algebra 1)
- Exit data: Advanced Placement assessments and graduation rate

Why SAT 11
A national norm-referenced test with consistent content over time (unlike M-STEP/MEAP variance), a leading college-admissions assessment, and vertically linked across grades 8-11 - enabling programmatic-impact tracking and state/county/school/student-group comparisons. Building-level results are shown against percent SED (socioeconomically disadvantaged).

Subcategory analysis
Math subcategories defined and compared: Heart of Algebra, Passport to Advanced Math, and Problem Solving and Data Analysis. Evidence-Based Reading & Writing subcategories: Command of Evidence, Expression of Ideas, Standard English Conventions, and Words in Context. Results are color-coded green (proficient/advanced), yellow (partially proficient), and red (not proficient). The deck cautions that system-level subcategory data is useful for spotting instructional trends but not for addressing individual student needs.

Math benchmarking changes
With a new K-8 math curriculum, the district will use PSAT 8 math as one growth measure and introduce NWEA this winter as a second, norm-referenced, computer-adaptive measure given during math class - replacing district-created benchmark assessments - with program evaluation in partnership with Illustrative Math.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A November 2023 board workshop presentation summarizing how the Troy School District measures and monitors student achievement, titled 'Student Assessment Data.' Its central theme is reviewing consistent measures over time, and it organizes the district's instruments into three buckets. Standardized assessments include the SAT Suite of Assessments, the SAT 11 (Scholastic Aptitude Test), the PSAT 8, and the M-STEP for grades 3-7. Instructional and benchmarking data include Fountas & Pinnell for ELA in grades K-5, CommonLit for ELA in grades 6-12, and NWEA for math from grade 6 through Algebra 1. Exit data comprise Advanced Placement assessments and the graduation rate.

The deck argues for the SAT 11 as a primary lens because it is a national norm-referenced assessment with consistent content and structure over time (contrasted with M-STEP/MEAP variance), is a leading collegiate-admissions assessment, and forms a suite with linkages from grade 8 to grade 11. These properties let the district observe programmatic impact over time, compare against state, county, school, and student-group results, and maintain transparency. Grade 11 SAT results are displayed by building, with buildings characterized by their percentage of SED (socioeconomically disadvantaged) students.

A substantial portion addresses subcategory analysis. For SAT/PSAT math, three subcategories are defined: Heart of Algebra (linear equations, systems, and functions), Passport to Advanced Math (structure of expressions, manipulation, and more complex equations and functions), and Problem Solving and Data Analysis (ratios, percentages, proportional reasoning, and interpreting data graphically and statistically). For Evidence-Based Reading and Writing, four subcategories are defined: Command of Evidence, Expression of Ideas, Standard English Conventions, and Words in Context. Subcategory comparison slides use a color key - green for proficient or advanced, yellow for partially proficient, and red for not proficient. The presentation notes that this subcategory review helps identify trends over time in narrow, focused areas of instruction, while cautioning that at the system level such data is not useful for addressing specific individual student learning needs.

The final section covers math benchmarking amid curriculum change. As the district moves forward with a new K-8 math curriculum, it will use PSAT 8 math performance as one data set to understand student growth over time. This winter it will introduce NWEA as a second data set for math performance; NWEA - a norm-referenced, computer-adaptive assessment administered nationally - will replace district-created benchmark assessments and will be given during the school day in students' math classes. The district also references engagement in program evaluation in partnership with Illustrative Math, and includes a PSAT 8 math subcategory comparison. Specific score values are presented in the slide charts and are not captured in the extracted text.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A November 2023 board workshop presentation reporting results of the Troy School District's school-calendar survey, which drew 3,460 respondents - 2,062 parents/guardians, 890 students, 360 staff, and 148 who were both. Across the respondent groups, reported satisfaction with the current calendar (extremely or somewhat happy) ranged from 58% to 79%. Majorities preferred starting school after Labor Day and keeping the current Winter Break and Mid-Winter Break lengths. The deck reviews legal requirements (180 days/1,098 hours), the Oakland County Common Calendar, and board and superintendent priorities.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
A 'Calendar Survey Results' board workshop deck (November 2023) presenting community feedback used to shape the Troy School District calendar.

Criteria considered
Federal/State/MDE guidance; superintendent's priorities; board priorities; the Oakland Schools county-wide recommended calendar; student and staff absentee data; and community/student/staff survey feedback.

Legal and priority framing
- Law: must provide 180 days or 1,098 hours of instruction.
- Board top priorities: a multi-year calendar for forward planning, alignment with surrounding districts, instructional continuity, data-driven decisions, legal compliance, and being respectful and inclusive of religious holidays.
- Oakland County Common Calendar: complies with School Aid Act sections 1284 and 1284b; recommends mid-winter breaks in the third week of February (President's Day week); spring break was moved up a week starting 2019-20 to separate it from MDE testing.

Survey response (3,460 total)
- 2,062 parent/guardian; 890 students; 360 staff; 148 both parent/guardian and staff.

Satisfaction
Across staff, students, parents/guardians, and parent-staff members, 'extremely happy & somewhat happy' responses were reported at 58%, 69%, 78%, and 79% (a 58%-79% range).

Highlights
All groups are relatively happy with the current calendar; all preferred full or half days off for professional development; majorities preferred starting after Labor Day and keeping the current Winter Break and Mid-Winter Break lengths.

Next steps
A Calendar Committee convenes in November; results feed into negotiations.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A November 2023 board workshop presentation reporting the results of the Troy School District's school-calendar survey and situating them within the legal and policy criteria that govern calendar design. The district frames the calendar work as a transparent, inclusive, and equitable process in which community input is central.

The deck first lists the criteria that shape the calendar: federal, state, and Michigan Department of Education guidance; the superintendent's priorities; the Board of Education's priorities; the Oakland Schools county-wide recommended calendar; student absentee data; staff absentee data; and community, student, and staff survey feedback. It notes the legal requirement to provide 180 days or 1,098 hours of instruction, and ties calendar choices to strategic-plan goals such as a deep and authentic sense of belonging, high-quality teaching and learning, adequate staffing, and professional-development opportunities.

The Board's stated top priorities are a multi-year calendar that allows forward planning, alignment with surrounding districts, instructional continuity, data-driven clarity in decisions, legal compliance, and being respectful and inclusive of religious holidays. Regarding the Oakland County Common Calendar, the presentation explains it is in compliance with sections 1284 and 1284b of the School Aid Act and sets, for the next five years, the dates when schools will not be in session for winter and spring holidays. Beyond the two legislated breaks, the Oakland County Superintendents Association (OCSA) recommends that districts with mid-winter breaks schedule them during the third week of February - President's Day week - regardless of length (currently two to five school days); the common calendar also moved spring break up a week beginning in 2019-2020 to provide a week between spring break and the MDE testing schedule.

The survey drew 3,460 total respondents: 2,062 parent/guardian, 890 students, 360 staff, and 148 who identified as both parent/guardian and staff. On overall satisfaction with the current calendar, the shares reporting 'extremely happy & somewhat happy' across the four respondent groups (staff, students, parents/guardians, and parents who are also staff) were 58%, 69%, 78%, and 79% - a range of 58% to 79%.

The survey highlights are that all groups are relatively happy with the current calendar; all groups preferred either full days or half days off for professional development; a majority preferred starting school after Labor Day; a majority preferred maintaining the current Winter Break length; and all groups wanted to keep the Mid-Winter Break the same length. For timeline and next steps, the district indicates a Calendar Committee convenes in November and that the results will be incorporated into negotiations. Precise per-response-option percentages beyond those noted are shown in the slide graphics and are not captured in the extracted text.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A board workshop accountability report presented in November 2023 under the banner 'Project 2026 Blueprint,' which tracks the Troy School District's progress against its 'World Class for All' pillars using an objectives-and-key-results structure and a 'See, Engage, Act' (re)design process. The extracted content details two of the pillars.

The Green Pillar, 'Early Childhood to Career,' sets objectives to continue investing in high-quality early childhood education - including advocating for access to universal preschool for all three- and four-year-olds - and to expand college and career pathways for middle and high school students, providing more access to high-quality career and technical education, expanding computer science, and connecting underrepresented students to in-demand, high-growth careers through partnerships with higher education, employers, and other stakeholders (work-based learning, credentials, and college credit). Reported key results and celebrations for June-November 2023 include 2023-24 early childhood enrollment figures: Tuition preschool capped at 240; GSRP at 98 (a 16-student increase, launching at Hill, Morse, Troy Union, and Wass); Strong Beginnings serving 14 TSD students in a free three-year-old program; PreK capped at 100 (an increase over 2022-23); and ECP capped at 96. Additional celebrations include the Fall 2023 launch of Portrait of a Learner; enhanced K-12 career readiness with expanded student portfolio work and maker-centered learning spaces (extending to the high school); post-secondary partnerships including an Early Middle College with Lawrence Technological University (LTU) and a Business Round Table; a Career Accelerator Program launched November 8, 2023; and a digital learning portfolio for grades 3-9 tied to Xello and future-ready career discussions. Noted challenges include recruitment and retention of highly qualified staff, identifying barriers to preschool access, aligning media/maker space with career readiness, and shifting the stigma around career readiness. Recommendations include continued preschool recruitment and access, expanding TSD learning portfolios to all students and parents in grades 3-9, prioritizing K-12 digital citizenship, and jumpstarting a K-12 computer science curriculum in collaboration with the Oakland Schools Computer Science team.

The Red Pillar, 'Equity and Well-Being,' sets objectives to ensure a focus on equity and well-being, fund additional investments to support the needs of the whole child, and elevate a district-wide focus on Alignment, Access, and Agency to meet the demands of a world-class learning environment in all school communities. Reported celebrations and key results (June-November 2023) include SEL curriculum expansion through continued pilots (Everyday Speech, Navigate 360, and Restorative Practices); SEL-focused programming such as Unified Sports, Advisory, Peer to Peer programs, tiered intervention, WEB, and Character.org; transforming adult SEL through affinity groups, a 'Dare to Lead' series, and professional learning; leadership professional learning via the Instructional Leadership Team (ILT); and elevating student experience through a Student Equity Council structure and Hanover. Hanover recommendations call for deeper professional learning for staff in equity, a heavy focus on issues of bullying, and prioritizing diversity - including district-wide resources and attention to gender identities and expression - alongside continued community engagement, cross-building equity teamwork, SEL curriculum and instruction, and MTSS consistency.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A November 7, 2023 memorandum from Assistant Superintendent Rick West to the Board's Policy Committee outlining recommended Policy Manual updates developed by Miller Johnson School Policy Services and the district Cabinet. Proposed changes include accommodating home-schooled students in non-essential elective classes (Policy 2000.01), stocking and administering opioid antagonists alongside epinephrine auto-injectors at every school building (Policy 2000.07/2007-AR), clarifying opt-out for physical exams and screenings, adding homebound/hospitalized instruction (Policy 3000.03), and updating pregnancy anti-discrimination language (Policy 4000.02). The Cabinet supports each change.

- 15.01 (Policy 2000.01, Admission and Enrollment): Add a 'Home Schooled Students' provision - the Board will attempt to accommodate home-schooled students who wish to take non-essential elective classes, consistent with law (MCL 380.1561; MCL 388.1766b). Cabinet supports.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A memorandum outlining recommended updates to the Troy School District Policy Manual, prepared for the Board's Policy Committee and included in the November 14, 2023 Special Meeting materials. The memo is from Rick West, dated November 7, 2023, and it summarizes revisions recommended by Miller Johnson School Policy Services together with the district's Cabinet team, organized by section of the Policy Manual, with explanations for each contemplated change and an action line recording positions of the Cabinet, Policy Committee, and Board of Education.

Update 15.01 concerns Policy 2000.01 (Admission and Enrollment). To eliminate confusion about supporting home-schooled students, new language would be added to the Resident Students section: 'Home Schooled Students. The Board will attempt to accommodate students who are home schooled and have a desire to take non-essential elective classes in the School District in a manner consistent with the law.' It cites MCL 380.1561 and MCL 388.1766b, and the Superintendent may develop administrative regulations. The Cabinet supports it.

Update 15.03 concerns Policy 2000.07 and Administrative Regulation 2007-AR (Health and Safety), combining opioid-antagonist language with the existing Epi-Pen policy. The revised policy provides that the district will acquire or purchase and maintain at least two functioning epinephrine auto-injectors (epi-pens) and at least one functioning opioid antagonist for and at each school building. Properly trained personnel or authorized contractors will administer an opioid antagonist to any individual on school grounds believed to be having an opioid-related overdose, and an epi-pen to anyone believed to be having an anaphylactic reaction or to a student with a prescription on file. The district will notify the parent of any student given an epi-pen or opioid antagonist, will encourage parents/guardians to seek treatment from a substance use disorder services program licensed under part 62 of the Public Health Code (1978 PA 368), and will call 911 in a believed overdose. The stated purpose is compliance with sections 1178 and 1179 of the Revised School Code, with administrative regulations incorporating the Michigan Department of Education's Medication Administration Guidelines by reference. The Cabinet supports adopting the language in its entirety.

Update 15.04 also concerns Policy 2000.07 (Health and Safety), adding a proviso that while annual notice and a parental opt-out will be given for physical examinations and screenings, this policy is not intended to apply to physical examinations required for sports participation. The Cabinet supports it.

Update 15.06 concerns Policy 3000.03 (Instruction), adding that the district will provide homebound and hospitalized instruction to qualified students consistent with federal/state law, with administrative regulations as needed. The Cabinet supports it.

Update 15.07 concerns Policy 4000.02 (Employment Considerations); citing two recent federal legislative changes that add clarity to the prohibition on discriminating against employees or prospective employees on the basis of pregnancy, it would update the Discrimination and Harassment policy within the Personnel section to ensure compliance (the extracted text is truncated here). The memo also notes there are no recommended updates for certain earlier sections, and it originates from the district's Business Office at 4400 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098 (phone 248-823-4022; fax 248-823-4013).
